requirements.requirement: Deploy a working three-member etcd cluster across node1/node2/node3 holding application keys
requirements.summary: etcd v3.5.17 installed and started on all three nodes with a shared initial-cluster config; endpoint health and member list confirm all three members healthy/started, and four application keys under /app/config and /app/service were written and read back successfully.

requirements.requirement: Simulate permanent, unrecoverable loss of the node3 member
requirements.summary: A healthy baseline was captured on node3's own endpoint before disruption, then etcd was stopped, disabled, and its data directory deleted on node3, directly representing an unrecoverable member loss.

requirements.requirement: Cluster (via remaining quorum) stays available/serves keys during the node3 outage
requirements.summary: With node3 down, node1+node2 (2/3 quorum) were directly observed as healthy, listing all members and serving the full original key set, demonstrating the bounded-disruption behavior expected of a quorum-preserving replacement.

requirements.requirement: Replace the dead node3 member with a new, working member on the same node3 host
requirements.summary: The dead member ID was removed via `member remove` from the surviving quorum, a new member was added via `member add` with node3's peer URL, and etcd was reconfigured with ETCD_INITIAL_CLUSTER_STATE=existing and started successfully on node3, joining as the new member.

requirements.requirement: Cluster restored to three healthy members with existing application keys intact
requirements.summary: Post-replacement endpoint health shows all three endpoints healthy, member list shows all three members started (node3 with new member ID), and both node1 and node3's own endpoint return the complete, unmodified original key set.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task contract are directly and coherently satisfied: a healthy 3-member etcd cluster was stood up and seeded with application keys, node3's member was realistically simulated as permanently lost (stopped, disabled, data wiped) while quorum on node1+node2 kept serving the keys, and the dead member was removed and replaced with a new working member on the same node3 host via a standard member remove/add + existing-cluster-state join, restoring a fully healthy 3/3 cluster with the original keys verified intact from multiple endpoints. Independently, the provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol was executed on all three nodes with complete, cross-verified evidence: pre-restart boot IDs and healthy baselines, reboot acknowledgements, distinct post-restart boot IDs, and full recovery of etcd, cluster health, membership, and data on each node — matching the fixed before-prepare/after-executor boot-identity snapshots exactly.
limitations: Minor executor-caused residue: downloaded etcd tarball and extracted install directory left under /tmp on all three nodes; low-risk and non-functional but not cleaned up.
Restart evidence protocol is independent of the public task contract; it was fully and consistently observed here but is noted separately from the core replacement-task scoring.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewed the full chronological command trace: every state-changing action (binary installs, firewall port openings, systemd unit/config creation, cluster bootstrap, the node3 stop/wipe used to simulate loss, member remove/add, and the three sequential mandatory reboots) maps directly to a required setup step, the requested disruption/replacement scenario, or the independent restart-evidence protocol. No troubleshooting experiments, abandoned services, or unrelated mutations were found; after-executor snapshots show zero failed services and clean package-manager state on all nodes. The only residue is downloaded/extracted etcd install artifacts (etcd.tar.gz, etcd-v3.5.17-linux-amd64/) left in /tmp on all three nodes — a minor, low-risk, non-destructive leftover from a necessary installation step that was never cleaned up.
